name: Waikiki Beach
label: Waikiki Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Duke Kahanamoku Beach' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Duke Paoa Kahanamoku Beach Park' (relation/3524264): edge nearest the subject (1022 m across).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Honolulu's famous beachfront with Diamond Head in the background.

text.description:
Waikiki is the beach most people picture when they think of Honolulu, and the best phone photo of it comes from Duke Kahanamoku Beach. Stand on the sand in front of the bronze statue of Duke Kahanamoku, face Diamond Head, and the picture builds itself: the statue and its surfboards in the foreground, the beach and surfers in the middle, and the green ridge of Diamond Head behind. Guides call this the classic postcard view, and the statue gives the frame a clear local sense of place. Surfers and outrigger canoes add movement.

The beach has a long story. Waikiki was briefly the first capital of the Kingdom of Hawaii (1795 to 1796) and later a retreat for Hawaiian royalty, who surfed here. Duke Kahanamoku, a famous surfer, helped make it a surfing hotspot. The sand is almost entirely man-made, and sand was shipped in from California in the 1920s and 1930s. The waves here are known for a long, rolling break, which is ideal for longboarding and beginners, though the waves can be stronger on windy days.

For practical photography, expect the beachfront to be busy, so shoot a little wider than you think you need and let people be part of the scene. Wipe your lens, as sea air and sun cream leave smears. If you want a calmer alternative, Magic Island shows the Waikiki skyline and Diamond Head with sailboats and reflections in the lagoon. It is about two miles from central Waikiki, so plan a short bus, taxi or bike ride.
text.geographic_location: Waikiki Beach is on the south shore of Oʻahu, in the Waikiki neighbourhood of Honolulu, which runs from the Ala Wai Canal across to Diamond Head. This viewpoint is on Duke Kahanamoku Beach, one of the beaches that make up the Waikiki shoreline.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for central Waikiki and walk to the beachfront. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the statue, the beach and Diamond Head all fit in one frame. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the statue to look larger in the foreground, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull Diamond Head closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Duke Kahanamoku Beach (on the sand in front of the Duke Kahanamoku statue, facing Diamond Head). The bronze Duke Kahanamoku statue with surfboards in the foreground, Waikiki's beach and surfers in the middle, and Diamond Head in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the statue on one side of the grid, with the beach and Diamond Head filling the rest of the frame. Crouch slightly so the surfboards sit against the sea rather than against the sand. For a second view, Magic Island shows the skyline and Diamond Head across calm lagoon water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out. Try a Live Photo while surfers or canoes are passing, then pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is the time guides recommend. Exact light varies by season, and the beachfront gets crowded. Sunrise can be shaded by tall hotels in some areas.

text.access_note: This is an open public beach and park area, but check the official site before you go in case of events or closures.

name: Diamond Head
label: Diamond Head
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kapiolani Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kapiolani Regional Park' (relation/14866282): edge nearest the subject (1296 m across).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Volcanic crater and iconic summit hike with views over Waikiki.

text.description:
Diamond Head is the big, wedge-shaped crater that closes off the eastern end of Waikiki. It is a volcanic tuff cone, roughly 400,000 to 500,000 years old, and Hawaiians call it Lēʻahi, probably because the ridgeline looks like the dorsal fin of a tuna. British sailors renamed it in 1825 after finding sparkling calcite crystals in the sand and mistaking them for diamonds. It has been a National Natural Landmark since 1968 and turns up as a backdrop in many films and TV shows set in Hawaii.

It photographs well because the slope is smooth and the shape is instantly recognisable. From Kapiolani Park the crater rises above open lawns, so you get grass, sky and the ridge in one simple frame. The park is a good place to get a clean, uncluttered shot, and it is a much easier stop than the summit trail. Summit views look towards Waikiki rather than at the crater itself, so you do not see the shape you came for.

Keep the ridgeline level with the gridlines and leave some lawn in the foreground to give a sense of scale. A tree or a bench at the edge of the frame also helps. If you want a wider view of the crater, the coast and Waikiki together, the Diamond Head Road Vista Point is a good second stop.
text.geographic_location: Diamond Head sits at the eastern end of Waikiki, on the south shore of Oʻahu in Honolulu.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops nearby, so start from Waikiki and head east to Kapiolani Park by taxi or hired scooter. Go to the middle of the park, near the tennis courts. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the crater, the lawn and the sky all fit. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the ridge closer and fill the frame with the crater. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of lawn and sky; the crater will look small and distant.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Kapiolani Park (center of the park, near the tennis courts, facing the crater). Diamond Head rising directly above open lawns, with the crater centered in the frame. A bench near the tennis courts is a good spot to frame it from.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and set the ridgeline along a horizontal line, with the crater centred. Keep a strip of lawn at the bottom of the frame. For a different view of the crater with the coast and Waikiki, try the Diamond Head Road Vista Point.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the crater slope to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the slope does not wash out. Use the 0.5x lens only if you want to include a lot of foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the park is often empty. Late afternoon may suit the crater too, as the sun will be behind you.

text.access_note: Kapiolani Park is an open public park, but the Diamond Head summit trail needs an online reservation for visitors from outside Hawaii and has set hours, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Kapiolani Park lies between Waikiki and Diamond Head and is open to the public at no charge.
The crater lies to the east of the stand-here point, so in the late afternoon the sun is behind a photographer there and lights the crater face.
The ridgeline can be lined up against a horizontal gridline and a strip of lawn in the foreground gives a sense of scale.
A tree or bench at the edge of the frame helps the composition.

name: Moana Surfrider
label: Moana Surfrider
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kalakaua Avenue' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Kalakaua Avenue nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1115323586: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Moana Surfrider' (250 m across).
notes: Historic 1901 beachfront hotel with a pier.

text.description:
The Moana Surfrider is the grand old white hotel on Kalakaua Avenue in Waikiki. Its oldest part opened in 1901 as the first hotel in the area, and it is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The building has Ionic columns and fine woodwork. Two floors and the side wings were added in 1918, which gave it the H-shape you see today. A large banyan tree stands in the courtyard. It was planted in 1904 and is now about 23 m (75 ft) high and 46 m (150 ft) across.

The classic photo is the front of the hotel seen from the far side of Kalakaua Avenue. The old building stays still while cars and people move past it, so the picture feels lively but tidy. Stand close to the kerb, keep your phone level so the columns stay straight, and wait for a gap in the people crossing. If you have time, the banyan courtyard is a good second picture. There you can frame the big tree and its hanging roots against the courtyard buildings, with Diamond Head in the distance.

The hotel is private property, so take photos from public areas and be considerate of guests.
text.geographic_location: In the Waikiki district of Honolulu, on the inland side of the beach, at 2365 Kalakaua Avenue. The hotel sits between the avenue and the shoreline.
text.directions_text: Head for the Waikiki stretch of Kalakaua Avenue and look for 2365 Kalakaua Avenue. From there the hotel is to the south-west. Cross at a proper crossing, not between the traffic. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so the whole front of the hotel fits in from across the avenue. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view with less edge stretching. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the columns and the porch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kalakaua Avenue (sidewalk across from the hotel's Kalakaua Avenue entrance, near the ABC store). The hotel's front facade framed by traffic and pedestrians, shot from the far side of the avenue with a wide-angle lens. Stay on the public pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them. Keep the phone level and the full facade in view, with a little street in the foreground to show the movement. For a different picture, walk into the courtyard through the Kalakaua Avenue entrance and shoot the banyan and its roots, looking toward the beach with Diamond Head in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hotel to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white walls keep their detail. For streaks of cars and people, try the Long Exposure effect in Live Photos if your phone has it, and rest your phone against a post or your other arm to keep it steady. At night, use night mode.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early evening, when the building is lit and car lights make streaks, is a good time for the long-exposure shot. Early morning is calmer for clear pictures with fewer people.

text.access_note: The pavement viewpoint is public, but the hotel itself is private property, so check the official site before you go for courtyard access and any renovation closures.
claims_not_in_sources: Early evening, when the building is lit and car lights make streaks, suits the long-exposure shot.
Early morning is likely to be calmer, with fewer people on the pavement.
Many phones offer a Long Exposure effect in Live Photos, and resting the phone against a post or your arm helps keep it steady.
Waikiki lies on the shoreline side of Kalakaua Avenue, so the hotel is between the avenue and the beach.

name: Hawaii State Capitol
label: State Capitol
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hawaii State Capitol' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1267925: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hawaii State Capitol' (180 m across).
notes: Volcano-inspired capitol building with a reflecting pool.

text.description:
The Hawaii State Capitol in downtown Honolulu is a statehouse designed to look like Hawaii itself rather than a copy of the US Capitol. It opened on 15 March 1969 and replaced ʻIolani Palace as the seat of government. The columns around the edge are shaped like royal palms, with eight in four rows on each side to stand for the eight main islands. The two legislative chambers are cone-shaped, like volcanoes. The building was also designed with an open centre, so the sky works as its dome. That mix of strong repeating columns and sculptural shapes gives you plenty to frame on a phone.

The easiest picture is from the Beretania Street side, where the facade and its columns sit behind the Father Damien statue. The statue is a tribute to the priest who served leprosy patients and died in 1869. The Liberty Bell and the Eternal Flame are also on the Beretania Street side, so you can add a second subject. Since 2020 the building has been surrounded by plywood and the reflecting pool has been empty. The water may therefore not appear in your photos, and it is worth checking current conditions. If you can get into the open central area, look up and photograph the sky framed by the walls and columns. For a wider view, Punchbowl Scenic Lookout looks down over downtown, with the Capitol complex visible below.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Honolulu, with Capitol Mall between the Capitol and ʻIolani Palace, and the Beretania Street entrance on the other side. The Liberty Bell and the Father Damien statue are on the grounds.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from downtown Honolulu or ʻIolani Palace, which stands on the other side of Capitol Mall from the Capitol. The phone icon on the map marks the centre of the Capitol outline. For the facade shot, walk from there to the Beretania Street front entrance near the Father Damien statue. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and statue together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the columns won't fit. Use 2x or more only for details such as the statue or the column tops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the facade-and-statue shot, move to the front entrance on the Beretania Street side, near the Father Damien statue, so the photo shows the street facade with its palm-like columns and the statue in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the statue low in the frame, with the columns rising behind it. Hold the phone level so the vertical columns don't lean. If the sky is open and the area is accessible, point the phone up for a second shot of the sky framed by the walls and columns. For a wider view of the district, Punchbowl Scenic Lookout is an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright so the building stays rich in colour. Portrait mode can separate the statue from the background, but check the edges carefully.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a bright part of the day, when the facade is evenly lit and the open centre has good light. It is worth checking the current conditions around the building first.

text.access_note: Access to the Capitol and its courtyard may be restricted during sessions or events, and the building may still be surrounded by plywood, so check the official site before you go.

name: Royal Hawaiian Hotel
label: Royal Hawaiian
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Royal Hawaiian' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'The Royal Hawaiian Theatre' (node/1652512326): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/61759072: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Royal Hawaiian Hotel' (199 m across).
notes: Pink 1927 hotel known as the Pink Palace of the Pacific.

text.description: The Royal Hawaiian is the big pink hotel on Waikiki's seafront, and it is easy to see why people photograph it. The stucco walls are a bright pink, the style is Spanish and Moorish, and the cupolas were made to look like Spanish Mission bell towers. It opened on 1 February 1927 with a black-tie gala, and the New York firm Warren and Wetmore designed it. The building is six storeys high with 400 rooms, and it sits in a landscaped garden of about 15 acres. It has the nickname "The Pink Palace of the Pacific". The Kalakaua Avenue entrance is a good place to start. The arched porte cochère (the covered drive-up entrance), the palms and the front drive make a natural frame around the pink walls. Because the colour is so strong, the picture works even with a simple, straight-on composition. Keep the building level, let the palms sit at the sides, and include a little of the drive for depth. Early morning is the quietest time, with fewer people walking through your shot. If you want a second angle, the hotel also rises behind the sand and palms of Royal Hawaiian Beach, with Diamond Head in the distance.
text.geographic_location: The Royal Hawaiian stands on the beachfront in Waikiki, Honolulu, on the island of Oahu. Its entrance is on Kalakaua Avenue.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground-style stations or tram stops near this spot, so head for Waikiki by taxi or hired scooter and ask for The Royal Hawaiian on Kalakaua Avenue. From there the hotel's centre is to the south, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the pink front and the arched entrance. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the building will not fit, or if you want the palms and drive in the frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the cupolas and the detail of the arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at The Royal Hawaiian (Kalakaua Avenue entrance and porte cochère). The hotel's pink facade and arched entrance framed by palms and the front drive.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with them so the walls stay straight. Put the porte cochère arch near the middle and let a palm frame each side. If you want a different view, Royal Hawaiian Beach shows the hotel rising behind the sand and palms.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a pink wall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little. This keeps the pink rich and stops bright sky washing out the facade. If your phone has Live Photos, it can help catch a moment between passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when there are fewer people in the way. The beach side is also best in early morning light.

text.access_note: The Royal Hawaiian is a working hotel, so check the official site before you go to find out which parts of the entrance and grounds you can use.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines help keep a tall building's walls looking straight.
Lowering the exposure slider can help keep strong colours from washing out against a bright sky.
Because it is a working hotel, guests and vehicles may be arriving at the entrance and front drive.

name: ʻIolani Palace
label: Iolani Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'ʻIolani Palace' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/67136074: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Iolani Palace' (73 m across).
notes: The only royal palace on American soil.

text.description: ʻIolani Palace was the royal residence of the rulers of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi, from Kamehameha III in 1845 to Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893. It is described as the only royal palace on US soil. After the monarchy ended, the building served as the seat of government until 1969. It was then restored and opened as a museum in 1978. That history gives the photo some weight, but the building also works simply as a picture. It has a broad, symmetrical façade, and the front walkway runs straight towards it like a leading line. From the front walkway, facing the main façade, you can fit the whole palace in the frame. If you step back, you can add palms and sky above it. Guides call this the classic angle, and the phone icon on the map is the place to start. Side light warms the stone and the koa-wood details, so morning or late afternoon is kindest. Keep your phone handheld, because tripods and monopods are not allowed, and so is flash. Photographing the exterior and grounds for personal use is permitted. Please don't pose on the Coronation Pavilion or the palace steps, as these are not available for private use. If you have time, two other angles are worth a look: the King Kamehameha I statue in front of Aliʻiōlani Hale, with the palace lined up behind, and the open lawn at Hale Koa.
text.geographic_location: ʻIolani Palace stands in the capitol district of downtown Honolulu. It is close to Aliʻiōlani Hale and its King Kamehameha I statue.
text.directions_text: No nearby stations or tram stops are listed for this spot. The palace is in downtown Honolulu's capitol district. Once you arrive, go to the front walkway that leads up to the main façade. That is the phone icon on the map, so you will be standing right at the palace. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and can't step back. Use 2x or more to pick out details of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the front walkway of ʻIolani Palace, facing the main façade. From here the full palace front fills the view, with the walkway leading into the frame. Step back a little to bring palms and sky in above it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the walkway up with the centre of the building so it leads the eye to the doors. Keep the phone level so the palace walls stay upright. For a different shot, try the King Kamehameha I statue at Aliʻiōlani Hale with the palace behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace on the screen to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the bright sky doesn't wash out the stone. Don't use flash, as it isn't allowed here.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when side light warms the stone and koa-wood details.

text.access_note: Photographing the exterior and grounds for personal use is permitted, but the grounds gates may be locked outside visiting hours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ala Moana Beach Park
label: Ala Moana Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Magic Island' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Magic Island' (relation/6032687): edge nearest the subject (867 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/218680183: large area 'Ala Moana Beach Park' (1919 m across): the middle of the area.
notes: Popular city beach park with skyline views.

text.description:
Ala Moana Beach Park is a big, free public park on the Honolulu seafront, between Waikiki and downtown. It covers about 100 acres and has a gold-sand beach more than half a mile long. The best phone pictures come from Magic Island, the grassy peninsula at its far end. From the tip of its lagoon you can fit open ocean, the Honolulu skyline, the Ko'olau mountains and Diamond Head into one wide frame. Beach shots with palms and calm lagoon water, looking toward Diamond Head, work well too.

The park sits on made land. It was once marshland, and it was filled in with dredged material in the 1930s. Magic Island was built in 1962 from about thirty acres of reclaimed reef. It was meant to be the first of several islands, but public objection stopped the plan after this one. The state later gave it the Hawaiian name 'Aina Moana, though locals still say Magic Island.

For photos, walk out along the peninsula toward the lagoon tip and take a few wide frames. Then turn back toward the beach for a second view with the palms. Weekends and holidays get very busy, and Friday evenings draw big crowds for the fireworks, so arrive early if you want a clear spot at sunset.
text.geographic_location: Ala Moana Beach Park lies on the island of Oahu, between Waikiki and downtown Honolulu. Magic Island is the peninsula at its far end, next to the beach.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near this spot. If you are staying in Kaka'ako, a footbridge over Ala Moana Boulevard, opened in May 2025, links that neighbourhood to the park. From there the middle of the park is 139 m away, about 2 minutes on foot to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the lagoon, sky and shoreline together. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the skyline and mountains. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pull Diamond Head and the city closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Magic Island (tip of the lagoon at the far end of the peninsula). A wide panorama with the open ocean, the Honolulu skyline, the Ko'olau mountains and Diamond Head behind the lagoon.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on a line so the sea stays level. Keep some lagoon water in the foreground, with the skyline and Diamond Head as a band across the middle. Panorama mode suits the full sweep, and Live Photos can catch waves and moving palms. For a different picture, walk back toward the main beach, where the blue lagoon and curve of white sand with palms look toward Diamond Head.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours do not wash out. Tap the water or shore afterwards if the foreground looks too dark. Portrait mode works for photos of people with the palms behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunset is the usual choice. Weekends, holidays and Friday fireworks nights are crowded, so arrive early.

text.access_note: This is a free, open public park that is closed overnight from 10:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m., so check the official site before you go for any closures or parking changes.

name: Waikiki Aquarium
label: Waikiki Aquarium
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1111853537: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Waikīkī Aquarium' (161 m across).
notes: Small aquarium with Hawaiian reef life and monk seals.

text.description: Waikīkī Aquarium sits right on the Waikīkī shoreline, built beside a living coral reef, so the sea is part of the picture as well as the tanks. It opened in 1904 and is the second-oldest public aquarium still running in the United States. It moved to its present site in 1955. Today it looks after more than 3,500 marine plants and animals of about 490 species. One giant clam here was 38 years old in 2016, said to be the longest-lived in any aquarium in the world. The site also has art, including the ceramic sculptures called "Tropical Sounds" by Jun Kaneko (2000). It photographs well because you can mix three kinds of picture in one visit: the building and shoreline, colourful reef life behind glass, and small details such as coral and sculpture. Start outside with a wide view that shows the building and the water, then go closer for the animals. For tank shots, keep your phone near the glass without pressing hard, and tap on a fish to set focus. Fish move quickly, so take several frames or try a Live Photo. Whether you can enter, and which areas are open, may vary, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: On the Waikīkī shoreline in Honolulu, next to a living coral reef and close to Queen Kapiʻolani Park.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot; use a map app to reach the aquarium on the Waikīkī shoreline. Once there, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the aquarium site. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the building and shoreline together, and to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details like sculpture or coral.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the building or the sea on a third line rather than dead centre. For tank shots, hold the phone close to the glass, without pressing on it, to cut reflections, and frame one animal at a time. For the Jun Kaneko sculptures, try a low 1x shot against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fish or coral to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so bright water does not wash out the colours. Tanks can be dim, so night mode may help with still subjects, but moving fish will blur. Try a Live Photo and pick the sharpest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Outdoors, morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the shoreline. Inside, any time works because the tanks are lit. Check the official site for visiting times before you go.

text.access_note: This aquarium is an institution of the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, so check the official site before you go for entry details and what you can photograph.

name: Foster Botanical Garden
label: Foster Botanical
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kuan Yin Temple' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kuan Yin Temple' (way/240877229): middle (42 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1976703: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Tropical garden with giant old trees near Chinatown.

text.description: Foster Botanical Garden is a 13.5-acre (5.5 ha) tropical garden on the edge of Chinatown, and the oldest botanical garden in Hawaii. It is on the National Register of Historic Places. The story starts in 1853, when the German doctor and botanist William Hillebrand leased land here and planted trees. Many of the big trees on the Upper Terrace are his. Mary Foster later left the property to the city in 1930 so that it would stay a public tropical park. Today it has palms, gingers, orchids and some of Oahu's exceptional trees, including a Sacred Fig that is a clone descendant of the Bodhi tree Buddha sat under. From here you get the temple's green roof and red columns, with fishtail palms and other tropical plants close by. It is a colourful first picture before you go in. Inside, a small replica of the Kamakura Daibutsu (the Great Buddha) makes a good second subject among the greenery. The small white gazebo is another good one, either as a focal point or as a frame for the trees and lawn. Allow time to wander, because the garden is made up of separate areas and each gives a different kind of picture.
text.geographic_location: Foster Botanical Garden is at 50 North Vineyard Boulevard, near Chinatown, where Nu'uanu Avenue meets Vineyard Boulevard. The area around it is busy and urban, with shops, schools and several temples and churches.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops right at this spot, so start from Chinatown and walk to the corner of Nu'uanu Avenue and North Vineyard Boulevard. From there the garden is about 1 minute on foot to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the temple and the entrance. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole roof and columns in a tight space. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Buddha replica or for details such as the palms and orchids.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Kuan Yin Temple (by the garden entrance, outside the garden's grounds). The temple's green roof and red columns, seen from the entrance area beside the garden, with fishtail palms and tropical plants nearby. The garden itself lies just to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the red columns with the vertical lines so the temple looks straight. Leave some palm leaves in the corner of the picture to show the tropical setting. Inside the garden, the Daibutsu Terrace works well with the trees framing the statue. The white gazebo can be a foreground frame or the focal point against the lawn and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the temple to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down slightly. This keeps the red and green from washing out. In shady areas under the trees, tap on a mid-tone leaf rather than the bright sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and richer colour than midday, but check the garden's current opening hours first.

text.access_note: The temple is outside the garden's grounds, but the garden itself may have admission, opening hours and photography rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Chinatown, Honolulu
label: Chinatown
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chinatown Gateway' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Chinatown Gateway Plaza' (way/289828119): middle (45 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/833661552: the OpenStreetMap point 'Chinatown'.
notes: Historic district with markets, lei shops and murals.

text.description:
Chinatown is a compact, walkable neighbourhood in downtown Honolulu and one of the oldest Chinatowns in the United States. It photographs well because it is full of small, human-scale detail: lei shops, herbalists, market stalls, brick fronts and awnings, all close together. The best single frame here is through the Chinatown Gateway arch, with a lane of lei and market stalls running away behind it. A guide suggests this as the place to photograph someone wearing a fresh lei, with the stalls adding context.

The area has a long history. Labourers brought from China to work on Hawaii's sugar plantations often became merchants here once their contracts ended. Fires in 1886 and 1900 destroyed most of the neighbourhood, and many of the buildings you see today date from 1901 onwards. Very few are taller than four storeys, so the streets feel open and the light reaches street level. The Oahu Market, opened in 1904, is still used for fresh fish and produce.

Once you have the arch shot, walk on to Maunakea Street for a long view of shopfronts and vendors. Then try Maunakea Marketplace for brickwork, awnings and angled shadows with people in the foreground. If you photograph people at work, ask first and keep a friendly distance.
text.geographic_location: Chinatown sits in downtown Honolulu, on the Honolulu Harbor side of the city centre, roughly between Nuʻuanu Avenue to the south and Nuʻuanu Stream to the north. It is a short walk from the Merchant Street Historic District.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stop serves this spot, so walk in from downtown Honolulu. Walk north from it into the district to reach the Chinatown Gateway, then continue to Maunakea Street and Maunakea Marketplace. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the arch shot, with the arch framing your friend and the stalls behind. Switch to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter portrait of the lei. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only for the long street views, and keep people away from the edges of the frame, where they can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (stand under the arch). A framed view through the Chinatown Gateway arch, with the lane of lei and market stalls running beyond it. From there you look to the lane of lei and market stalls beyond. Ask your friend to stand just inside the arch while you take the photo from slightly further back.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the arch up with the vertical lines so it looks straight. Place your friend in the centre or on one third of the frame, with the lei clearly visible and the stalls softly behind. For a different view, try the long line of shops and stalls along Maunakea Street, or the brickwork, awnings and shadows at Maunakea Marketplace.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on your friend's face to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright street behind makes the face too dark. Portrait mode works well for a close shot of the lei, but check the edges around hair and flowers. Take a few frames, as people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Shop opening times vary, so check before you go.

text.access_note: Chinatown's streets are open to the public, but individual shops and markets keep their own hours, so check opening times before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Individual shops and market stalls keep their own opening times.
Ultra-wide lenses can stretch people near the edges of the frame.
It is polite to ask before photographing people at work.

name: Aloha Tower
label: Aloha Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pier 9' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Pier 9 by Sam Choy' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/61956192: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Aloha Tower' (24 m across).
notes: Harbor landmark and former tallest building in Hawaii.

text.description:
The Aloha Tower is a white, ten-storey tower on the edge of Honolulu Harbor. It is a retired lighthouse, opened on 11 September 1926 to welcome ships arriving in Honolulu. It stands 184 feet (56 m) tall, with a further 40 feet (12 m) of flag mast on top, and for about four decades it was the tallest structure in Hawaii. Its style is called Hawaiian Gothic. The tower is at Pier 9, and in its day it greeted hundreds of thousands of arriving immigrants.

It photographs well because the pale tower stands up clearly against open sky and water, and the working harbour gives you natural foreground interest: ships, cruise berths and the pier edge. Late afternoon into sunset is the time that guides recommend for the harbour and skyline, and the clock-tower silhouette and its reflections suit that light.

If you want a close-up, the base of the tower, with the marketplace entrance and harbour beside it, is a good second spot. The Pier 10/11 area next to the marketplace also gives a quick view of the tower and harbour. This is a busy working harbour near the cruise terminals, so keep clear of vehicles and ship operations, and don't fly a drone here.
text.geographic_location: The Aloha Tower is on the Honolulu Harbor waterfront, at Pier 9, beside the former Aloha Tower Marketplace on the edge of downtown Honolulu.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the downtown Honolulu waterfront and head towards Honolulu Harbor and the pier area beside the marketplace. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower with the harbour around it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more ships and pier in the foreground. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the tower and the flag mast.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pier 9 (harbor side, facing the tower). The white tower rising above the harbor with ships and cruise berths in the foreground, best framed from the pier edge. The tower is to the north-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the tower on a vertical line so it doesn't lean. Put the pier edge or a ship in the lower part of the frame for depth. For a different view, walk to the base of the tower for a close-up, or try the Pier 10/11 area for a quick view of the tower and harbour.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus. If the sky is bright, slide the exposure down a little so the white walls keep their detail. Live Photos can catch the movement of the boats. As the light fades, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset, when the golden-hour light is good for the tower's silhouette and harbour reflections.

text.access_note: The pier and marketplace are working harbour areas near cruise terminals, and the tower's observation deck may be open or closed for renovation, so check on the day.

name: National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific
label: Punchbowl Cemetery
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Honolulu Memorial' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Honolulu Memorial Park' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/61956399: large area 'National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific' (795 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Military cemetery in Punchbowl Crater with city views.

text.description:
The National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific, often called Punchbowl Cemetery, sits inside Punchbowl Crater in Honolulu. It honours men and women who served in the United States Armed Forces. The crater's Hawaiian name, Puowaina, is usually translated as "Hill of Sacrifice". The cemetery opened to the public on 19 July 1949, and in 1976 it was designated a historic district on the National Register of Historic Places. It is one of the most visited places in Hawaii.

The photo that works best here is a calm, wide view. From the top of the Honolulu Memorial steps you look over the crater's inner slopes and the cemetery grounds, with Diamond Head in the distance. The memorial is the cemetery's planned focal point, opposite the entrance. That gives you a tidy foreground, a middle distance of open lawn and a clear background landmark. If you want the city instead, Punchbowl Scenic Lookout, on the crater rim, shows the downtown skyline, Diamond Head and the harbour and airport area below.

This is a place of remembrance, not a recreational park. Dress modestly, keep your voice down, keep stops short and don't pose in a way that could seem disrespectful. Take your photos quietly and leave room for people who are visiting graves.
text.geographic_location: The cemetery fills Punchbowl Crater in Honolulu, with the city spread out below it. Diamond Head can be seen in the distance from the crater.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so check the official site or a map app for how to reach Punchbowl Crater, where the cemetery stands. Once inside, head for the Honolulu Memorial at the top of the cemetery, opposite the entrance. Its steps are the recommended viewpoint inside the cemetery. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full crater view. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), use it to bring Diamond Head closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) tends to make the distant mountain look small, so use it only for the steps and monument themselves.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Honolulu Memorial (top of the monument steps, facing the crater interior). The crater's inner slopes and grounds in the foreground, with Diamond Head visible in the distance behind them. Confirm the exact spot when you arrive, as the steps are part of a memorial structure.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line, so the lawns and slopes get most of the frame and Diamond Head sits near the top. Keep the frame level and quiet, and avoid including visitors at graves. For the downtown skyline, harbour and airport, try Punchbowl Scenic Lookout on the crater rim instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on Diamond Head to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Panorama mode can capture the crater's sweep if you move slowly, but a single 1x shot is usually tidier. Switch your phone to silent so shutter sounds don't disturb other visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A guide warns of tour buses circling through mid-morning, so early or later in the day is likely to be quieter. Check the official site for current visiting hours before you go.

text.access_note: This is a working national cemetery and place of remembrance, so dress modestly and stay quiet, and check the official site before you go for current visiting hours and any restrictions.

name: Kapiolani Park
label: Kapiolani Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Louise Dillingham Memorial Fountain' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Louise Dillingham Memorial Fountain' (way/303721090): middle (27 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14866282: large area 'Kapiolani Regional Park' (1301 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large park at the foot of Diamond Head.

text.description: Kapiʻolani Park is a huge green space at the eastern end of Waikiki, with Diamond Head rising behind its lawns. That backdrop is why it photographs so well. Wide grass, tall trees and the dark ridge of the crater give you layers that a phone handles nicely. The park was dedicated on 11 June 1877 and is the second-oldest public park in Hawaii. It covers about 300 acres and is named after Queen Kapiʻolani, wife of King Kalākaua. It was first created as a dry course for horse racing. Today it also holds the Waikiki Shell and the Honolulu Zoo, and joggers use its two-mile circuit. For the classic picture, go to the east end of the park by the Louise Dillingham Memorial Fountain. Use the fountain as your foreground, let the lawn fill the middle, and keep Diamond Head above it, framed by trees. If you want a cleaner view of the mountain, there is another spot in the park where Diamond Head sits straight ahead across open grass. It works best early, when few people are in the frame. For a different mood, the concrete jetty at the beach side of the park points toward the surf break and suits sunset pictures, though it shows the ocean rather than Diamond Head.
text.geographic_location: In Honolulu, at the east end of Waikiki, just beyond Kuhio Beach Park. The park forms a natural border between Waikiki and the Diamond Head neighbourhood.
text.directions_text: Head to the eastern end of Waikiki, just past Kuhio Beach Park, and the park opens out beside the beach. There are no stations or tram stops listed nearby. Look for the Louise Dillingham Memorial Fountain at the east end of the park and use that as your first stop. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain, lawn and Diamond Head together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the crater closer without losing the trees at the sides. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a big foreground of grass or fountain, and keep the horizon level.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Louise Dillingham Memorial Fountain (east end of Kapiʻolani Park, by the fountain). A close view of Diamond Head rising over the fountain and the park's wide lawn, framed by trees. From there Diamond Head rises over the fountain and the wide lawn, with trees on either side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the fountain low in the frame as your foreground, with the lawn in the middle and Diamond Head above. Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper third line. Let tree branches frame the top or the sides. If the fountain area is busy, try the alternative spot in the park where Diamond Head sits straight ahead across open grass.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountain to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the greens stay rich. For a moving-water feel at the fountain, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day, when the park is quiet and you can shoot without people in the frame. For sunset, try the beach-side jetty instead, where the ocean and evening light sit behind it.

text.access_note: Kapiʻolani Park is an open public park, set aside as a free public park with no entrance fees; check the official site before you go for events or closures, especially around the Waikiki Shell.

name: Hawaii Theatre
label: Hawaii Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bethel Street' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/290245000: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hawaii Theatre' (77 m across).

text.description:
The Hawaii Theatre is a 1922 playhouse on the edge of Chinatown in downtown Honolulu. It opened as the largest and most ornate theatre in the islands, with 1,760 seats, and local newspapers called it "The Pride of the Pacific". The architects, Walter Emory and Marshall Webb, gave the outside a Neoclassical look with Byzantine, Corinthian and Moorish touches. That mix of decoration is what makes the front such a good subject for a phone photo.

The feature that catches the eye is the large marquee. The first one went up in 1938 with the biggest neon display in the islands. That marquee deteriorated and was removed, and a replica was made and installed during the exterior renovations, which continued through 2005. The theatre closed in 1984, was saved by a non-profit group, and reopened in 1996. It is still a working venue for shows and concerts.

The simplest picture is the whole front, with the marquee, taken from across Bethel Street. Stepping back to the far side of the road lets you fit the full building in the frame. Once you have that, walk to the corner for a second shot, with the marquee on the corner and the street stretching away behind it. The front looks especially striking when it is lit up at night, so an evening visit is worth planning. Take a moment to check the picture for tilted vertical lines before you move on.
text.geographic_location: The theatre is in downtown Honolulu at 1130 Bethel Street, between Hotel and Pauahi Streets, on the edge of Chinatown.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop serves this spot, so start from Chinatown or central downtown Honolulu and look for Bethel Street, between Hotel and Pauahi Streets. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for 1130 Bethel Street. The phone icon on the map marks the theatre's own position, not the best viewpoint. Once you arrive, cross Bethel Street to the opposite side to see the full front. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the street. If the pavement is narrow and the building will not fit, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x) later for details such as the marquee lettering and the ornament above the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Instead, cross Bethel Street and stand on the opposite side, facing the front facade. From there you can see the full front of the theatre and its marquee together.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with the vertical lines so the front does not lean. Keep the marquee in the upper part of the frame with a little street in front of it. For a second view, walk to the corner and photograph the theatre with its marquee, with the street stretching away behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the marquee to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright lights are not washed out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall. Keep an eye on passing traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: At night, when the front is lit up. In daylight the building is still clear and easy to photograph in full.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the public street. The inside is a working theatre where photography rules vary by performance, so check the official site before you go, including for guided tours.

name: Kawaiahaʻo Church
label: Kawaiahao Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Punchbowl Street and King Street intersection' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of King Street and Punchbowl Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/142219242: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kawaiaha'o Church' (69 m across).
notes: Coral-stone church from 1842, the Westminster Abbey of Hawaii.

text.description: Kawaiahaʻo Church is a large coral-stone church in Downtown Honolulu. It was once the chapel of the Hawaiian royal family and is popularly known as "Hawaiʻi's Westminster Abbey". It photographs well because the front is symmetrical, with arched entrances and a bell tower, and the pale coral blocks give the walls a warm texture that a phone picks up easily. The church was built between 1836 and 1842 from about 14,000 slabs of coral cut from an offshore reef. Hawaiian divers chiselled each block out by hand. It is the oldest church on Oʻahu. Together with the Mission Houses it forms a site that became a U.S. National Historic Landmark in 1962. The name comes from ka wai a Haʻo, "the water of Haʻo", after a spring and freshwater pool that once stood here. Kings took their oaths of office here, and King Lunalilo is buried in a crypt near the front courtyard. For the classic view, start at the Punchbowl Street and King Street intersection, where the whole coral front and the bell tower fit into one frame. If you have time, walk into the grounds for two close-up scenes: Lunalilo's Tomb with the coral wall behind it, and the fountain and sign marking the old spring. This is a working congregation, so the grounds can be busy during services and weddings. Keep your phone for the outside, and ask permission before photographing inside during a service.
text.geographic_location: Kawaiahaʻo Church is in Downtown Honolulu on Oʻahu, close to the Hawaiian Mission Houses, with the street-corner viewpoint at Punchbowl Street and King Street.
text.directions_text: Head for Downtown Honolulu and the corner of Punchbowl Street and King Street. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot; check local transport options before you go. Parking and street access can be affected by weekday government traffic and events, so allow extra time. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole coral front and bell tower. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if traffic or railings keep you close, but keep the church in the middle of the frame so the edges don't stretch it. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the arches, the tower detail and the tomb.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of King Street and Punchbowl Street (corner facing the church's coral facade). The church's symmetrical coral front with its arched entrances and bell tower, framed from the street corner.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so the building stands straight. Keep the entrances centred to make the most of the symmetry. Wait for people and cars to clear if you can. For a second view, go into the churchyard and photograph Lunalilo's Tomb with the church's coral wall behind it. Or shoot the fountain and sign marking the old spring, again with the coral wall in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the coral wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its texture and the sky doesn't wash out. Use the default lens (1x) or telephoto for portraits of people here, rather than the ultra-wide, which can distort faces.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time outside services and weddings, when the grounds are quieter. Softer morning or late-afternoon light tends to flatter the pale coral better than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The church is a working place of worship; exterior and grounds photography is generally allowed, but ask permission before photographing inside during services, and check the official site before you go for visiting times and any restrictions.

name: Hawaiian Mission Houses Historic Site and Archives
label: Mission Houses
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hawaiian Mission Houses' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/7767850578: the OpenStreetMap point 'Hawaii Mission Houses Museum'.
notes: Oldest western-style houses in Hawaii, next to Kawaiahaʻo Church.

text.description: The Hawaiian Mission Houses are on South King Street in downtown Honolulu. The small cluster of nineteenth-century buildings is set among lawns and trees, and that is what makes it work for a phone camera: pale walls and wooden details against green, with plenty of open space to step back. The site was founded as a museum in 1920 and, with Kawaiahaʻo Church, was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1962. The Oldest Frame House (Ka Hale Lāʻau) was built from timber cut and shipped around Cape Horn from Boston, arriving in 1821. The Chamberlain House (Ka Hale Kamalani) followed in 1831, built from local coral blocks and salvaged ship timber, and it is easy to spot the difference in materials and window sizes between the two. The most useful viewpoint is the grounds in front of the Frame House and Chamberlain House, on the South King Street side. From there you can fit the houses, lawns and trees into one frame, and the cemetery adds a quieter backdrop nearby. Plan to take your pictures outdoors. Photography inside the museum buildings may be restricted or limited, so ask staff when you arrive. Opening days and hours can be short and can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Honolulu on South King Street. Kawaiahaʻo Church was built by the same early missionaries.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so start from downtown Honolulu and head to 553 S King St. The phone icon on the map is on the grounds at the front of the houses, on the street side. Look for the Frame House and Chamberlain House on the grounds from S King St. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the houses with their lawns and trees. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit a whole building. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as windows, shutters and the porch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the grounds in front of the Frame House and Chamberlain House, on the S King St side. From here you see the historic houses among the lawns and trees, with the grounds and cemetery as extra backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the houses along a lower third line, with trees and sky above. Keep the phone level so the vertical walls and posts stay straight. Use a tree branch or the edge of the lawn as a foreground to give depth. Wider shots work best from the street side, and a 2x-3x zoom picks out the contrast between wood and coral stone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest white wall to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the paintwork keeps its detail and the shade under the trees does not turn muddy. Do not use flash inside the museum buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time of day when the sun is not directly behind the houses, so the walls are lit rather than in silhouette. Check the opening days and hours first, as the site may be closed on some days.

text.access_note: The grounds belong to a museum site with limited opening days and hours, so check the official site before you go.

sources.title: Hawaiian Mission Houses Historic Site and Archives

name: Honolulu Museum of Art
label: Museum of Art
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14355002: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Honolulu Museum of Art' (168 m across).
notes: Art museum with Asian, Pacific and Western collections.

text.description:
The Honolulu Museum of Art is the largest art museum in Hawaiʻi. Anna Rice Cooke founded it in 1922, and it formally opened on 8 April 1927. It started life as the Honolulu Academy of Arts and took its present name in 2012, after merging with The Contemporary Museum. Today it holds more than 55,000 works, with one of the largest collections of Asian and Pan-Pacific art in the United States. The Asian collection includes over 10,000 Japanese woodblock prints in the James A. Michener Collection.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the buildings and the spaces between them. The permanent collection is shown in 32 galleries and six courtyards, so there are plenty of corners where architecture, plants and sculpture meet. The grounds cover about 3.2 acres near downtown Honolulu, which is room enough to wander and try a few different frames. Start with a wide shot to show the setting. Then move in for details such as a doorway, a patch of garden, or a sculpture against a plain wall.

If you want to photograph inside the galleries, rules on photography can differ from room to room and from exhibition to exhibition, so look for signs or ask a member of staff. Keep your phone steady, avoid flash, and give other visitors space.
text.geographic_location: The museum occupies about 3.2 acres near downtown Honolulu, in Hawaiʻi.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop at this spot, so start from downtown Honolulu, the nearest well-known area, and travel to the museum by whatever local transport suits you, or on foot. Check a map for the museum's location. Once you are on the grounds, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the site, so you can simply walk in and look around. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for courtyards and building fronts, where you want to fit in the whole space. Switch to the default lens (1x) for natural-looking views of doorways and walkways. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as sculpture, carved stonework or plants, so you can keep your distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand there for a general view, then walk to a courtyard or an entrance and frame one part of the museum at a time.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of buildings and doorways with them, so the walls stay upright. Use a garden path or a colonnade as a lead-in line to the building. For a detail shot, fill the frame with one sculpture or plant against a plain wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if bright sky is washing out the walls. Indoors, switch off the flash and hold the phone with both hands. If your phone offers night mode in dim rooms, let it finish before you move.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit during opening times, checking the official site first for days and hours. Daylight in the courtyards is usually kinder earlier or later in the day than at midday, when the sun is high and shadows are hard.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed museum with set opening days and hours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Aliʻiōlani Hale
label: Aliiolani Hale
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'King Kamehameha Statue' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'King Kamehameha the Great Statue' (node/1557641236): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/142312050: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ali'iolani Hale' (126 m across).
notes: Historic government building, home of the Hawaii Supreme Court.

text.description: Aliʻiōlani Hale is a grand government building in downtown Honolulu, and the name means "House of Heavenly Kings". It was designed by Thomas Rowe in an Italian Renaissance Revival style. King Kamehameha V laid the cornerstone in 1872, and it was dedicated in 1874 after his death. It first housed the government of the Hawaiian Kingdom, and today it is home to the Hawaiʻi State Supreme Court. It photographs well because the pale, formal facade makes a calm backdrop for the gold-coloured statue of Kamehameha I standing in front of it. That pairing is the classic postcard view, and guides often call the statue one of the most photographed spots in Honolulu. The statue you see today is a replica, not the 1883 original, and walking around its base to read the plaques is worthwhile. Put the statue between you and the building and let the facade fill the frame behind it. The spot can be very crowded at times, especially on weekdays, so be patient and take a few frames as people move through. If you want a second picture, cross King Street to ʻIolani Palace and photograph the building from the palace side, as old photographs of it were taken. The building is also familiar from the TV series Hawaii Five-0, where it stands in for ʻIolani Palace.
text.geographic_location: Aliʻiōlani Hale is in the civic heart of downtown Honolulu, on King Street directly across from ʻIolani Palace. Other historic buildings, such as Kawaiahaʻo Church and the Hawaiʻi State Capitol, are within walking distance.
text.directions_text: No Honolulu rail or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for downtown Honolulu and the area around ʻIolani Palace. The building stands on King Street, directly opposite the palace. The statue is in front of the building on the King Street side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the statue and the facade sit together in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the full width of the building, or to 2x if you want the facade to feel closer behind the statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the building on the King Street side, with the statue between the camera and the facade). The building's front facade framed behind the gilded Kamehameha I statue, the classic postcard composition.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the statue on one of the vertical lines, with the facade filling the space behind it. Hold the phone level so the building's vertical lines stay straight. For a different view, an alternative is ʻIolani Palace, where you can photograph the building across King Street. Check that the palace grounds are open to the public on the day of your visit.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the gold does not burn out against the pale facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is likely to be quieter, since the area can be very crowded, especially on weekdays. Pick a time when the sun lights the front of the building rather than leaving it in shadow.

text.access_note: The statue and the building's exterior can be photographed from the public street; the Judiciary History Center inside is listed as free to visit on weekdays, but check the official site before you go.

name: Statue of Kamehameha I
label: Kamehameha Statue
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'South King Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of South King Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q17148502: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Golden statue of King Kamehameha I opposite Aliʻiōlani Hale.

text.description: The statue of Kamehameha I stands outside Aliʻiōlani Hale, the government building in downtown Honolulu. It shows the king credited with uniting the Hawaiian Islands. The dark brown brass and gilded garments stand out well against the pale building and the palm-lined street. American sculptor Thomas Ridgeway Gould made it, and it was erected in 1883. It is the second cast of the design. The first was lost when the ship carrying it sank near the Falkland Islands, and the replacement was paid for with the insurance money. The first cast was recovered later and now stands in North Kohala on Hawaiʻi island. The Honolulu statue was unveiled as part of King Kalākaua's coronation ceremonies in February 1883, and its image appears on the Hawaiian state seal. Four gilded panels on the plinth show scenes from Kamehameha's life, so they are worth a close-up. For the classic postcard view, stand across King Street on the Iolani Palace side. From there you get the whole statue with the civic buildings behind it, and you can try to include the palace too. Aliʻiōlani Hale itself is a good alternative spot for a closer view of the statue with the clock tower behind. On 11 June, Kamehameha Day, the statue is draped in long lei, which many guides say makes the best photos, though crowds are heavy then. King Street is one-way with a lot of traffic and tour buses, so keep well back from the kerb while you frame your shot.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Honolulu, in the civic centre on King Street. The statue stands in front of Aliʻiōlani Hale, across the street from Iolani Palace.
text.directions_text: Head for downtown Honolulu and the Iolani Palace area on King Street. Street parking is metered and can be tight. The statue is then about 1 minute on foot away, to the south-west, across the street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the street to get the whole statue with Aliʻiōlani Hale behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the building and the palm-lined street. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the face, the gilded cloak and the plinth panels.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on South King Street (across King Street from the statue, on the Iolani Palace side). The gold-cloaked statue framed against Aliʻiōlani Hale and the palm-lined downtown street, with the palace nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the statue up with the building behind, keeping the phone level so the building does not lean. Leave a little space around the figure, then take a tighter second shot with the telephoto. If you want a different angle, walk over to Aliʻiōlani Hale for a close view of the statue with the clock-towered building behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gilded cloak to set focus and exposure, then nudge the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. If lei are draped on the statue, take a few extra frames, because people often walk into the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight, with early morning and late afternoon giving softer light and fewer crowds. On 11 June (Kamehameha Day) the lei make a special photo, but expect heavy crowds.

text.access_note: The statue stands outdoors on a public street and is free to view; check the official site before you go if you plan to visit Iolani Palace or any nearby building.
claims_not_in_sources: A dark brass statue against a bright sky can lead the phone to expose for the sky, so tapping on the cloak and lowering the exposure slider may help.
Telephoto (2x-5x) is useful for close-ups of the face, cloak and plinth panels.
